claim: Existing epidemiological simulation tools have limited resolution or can only account for a limited number of agents.
source: However, existing tools have limited resolution or can only account for a limited number of agents.
evidence: This is stated as background context without specific supporting data in the manuscript, drawing on general knowledge of the field.

claim: Epidemap can capture the daily movement of more than 60 million people in a country at a building-level resolution.
source: We introduce Epidemap, a new framework that can capture the daily movement of more than 60 million people in a country at a building-level resolution in a realistic and computationally efficient way.
evidence: This is a description of the capabilities of the Epidemap framework developed in this study.

claim: Epidemap simulations uncover the emergence of two distinct peaks in the daily number of cases for an infectious disease spreading in France.
source: By applying it to the case of an infectious disease spreading in France, we uncover hitherto neglected effects, such as the emergence of two distinct peaks in the daily number of cases or the importance of local density in the timing of arrival of the epidemic.
evidence: This finding is supported by simulation results presented in the manuscript.

claim: Local density is important in the timing of arrival of the epidemic.
source: By applying it to the case of an infectious disease spreading in France, we uncover hitherto neglected effects, such as the emergence of two distinct peaks in the daily number of cases or the importance of local density in the timing of arrival of the epidemic.
evidence: This finding is supported by simulation results presented in the manuscript.

claim: The importance of super-spreading events strongly varies over time during an epidemic.
source: Finally, we show that the importance of super-spreading events strongly varies over time.
evidence: This finding is supported by simulation results presented in the manuscript.

claim: Mathematical modelling is a powerful tool to describe infectious disease epidemics when combined with statistical modelling.
source: Mathematical modelling is a powerful tool to describe infectious disease epidemics, for example when combined to statistical modelling, and also to understand ongoing processes (Kermack and McKendrick, 1927; Keeling and Rohani, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established literature in the field.

claim: The COVID-19 pandemic highlighted the importance of mathematical epidemiology models for elaborating intervention strategies.
source: The recent COVID-19 pandemic has put in the spotlights the importance of mathematical epidemiology models to elaborate intervention strategies (Adam, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Adam, 2020.

claim: In the initial stages of an outbreak, the effect of spatial structure is minimal because transmission chains are largely independent.
source: In the initial stages of an outbreak, the effect of spatial structure is minimal because transmission chains are largely independent, but individual heterogeneity and stochasticity have major effects (Trapman et al., 2016; Britton and Scalia Tomba, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Trapman et al., 2016 and Britton and Scalia Tomba, 2019.

claim: Individual heterogeneity and stochasticity have major effects in the initial stages of an outbreak.
source: In the initial stages of an outbreak, the effect of spatial structure is minimal because transmission chains are largely independent, but individual heterogeneity and stochasticity have major effects (Trapman et al., 2016; Britton and Scalia Tomba, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Trapman et al., 2016 and Britton and Scalia Tomba, 2019.

claim: As an epidemic unfolds and hosts become immune, accounting for the exact shape of local contact networks matters increasingly.
source: As the epidemic unfolds and host become immune, accounting for the exact shape of local contact networks matters increasingly (Keeling and Rohani, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Keeling and Rohani, 2008.

claim: Agent-based simulations are very computationally demanding, which restrains the total number of agents that can be simulated.
source: First, ABS are very computationally demanding (Eubank et al., 2004), which restrains the total number of agents that can be simulated.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Eubank et al., 2004.

claim: Smieszek et al., 2011 analyzed the spread of influenza virus in Switzerland using an agent-based simulation with a grid resolution of 500x500m.
source: There are exceptions and, for instance, Smieszek et al., 2011 analyse the spread of influenza virus in Switzerland using an ABS using a grid with 500x500m resolution.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Smieszek et al., 2011.

claim: Rockett et al., 2020 performed an analysis of epidemic spread in Australia using 2310 level 2 statistical areas.
source: Rockett et al., 2020 perform a similar analysis in Australia using the 2310 level 2 statistical areas
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Rockett et al., 2020.

claim: A typical Epidemap simulation generates daily mobility patterns for 66 million individuals at the scale of buildings and lasts less than 2 hours.
source: A typical simulation generates daily mobility patterns for 66 million individuals at the scale of buildings and lasts less than 2 hr.
evidence: This is a description of the computational performance of the Epidemap platform.

claim: In Epidemap simulations, each individual is assigned to a residency building and can visit two other buildings every day.
source: In the simulations, which are summarised in Figure 1 and detailed in the Materials and methods, each individual is assigned to a residency building and can visit two other buildings every day.
evidence: This is a description of the simulation methodology.

claim: Buildings visited by individuals in Epidemap are chosen at random based on a distance kernel.
source: These buildings are chosen at random based on a distance kernel (see the Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a description of the simulation methodology.

claim: Transmission can occur in Epidemap when more than one individual visits the same building on the same day.
source: If more than one individual visits the building the same day, transmission can occur.
evidence: This is a description of the transmission mechanism in the simulation.

claim: The life-history of the infection in Epidemap is parameterised using data from the COVID-19 epidemic in France.
source: The life-history of the infection is parameterised using data from the COVID-19 epidemic in France (Sofonea et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Sofonea et al., 2021.

claim: Epidemap simulations assume that recovered individuals have perfect immunity for the duration of the simulation.
source: Given the general scope of this study, we assume that recovered individuals have perfect immunity for the duration of the simulation (i.e. a classical Susceptible Infected Recovered (SIR) epidemiological formalism)
evidence: This is a stated assumption of the model.

claim: All Epidemap simulations are initialised with 15 infected individuals in Paris to avoid premature random epidemic extinction.
source: and that all simulations are initialised with 15 infected individuals in Paris to avoid premature random epidemic extinction.
evidence: This is a description of the initial conditions used in the simulations.

claim: The basic reproduction number (R0) in the Epidemap simulations is of the order of 3.
source: With our minimal parameterisation, we see that the basic reproduction number, which is denoted (R0) and corresponds to the average number of secondary infections caused by an infected individual (Anderson and May, 1991), is of the order of 3, which is consistent with estimates for the French epidemic (Salje et al., 2020; Sofonea et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a result from the simulations, with citations to Anderson and May, 1991 for the definition and Salje et al., 2020 and Sofonea et al., 2021 for comparison.

claim: The R0 value of approximately 3 in Epidemap simulations is consistent with estimates for the French COVID-19 epidemic.
source: With our minimal parameterisation, we see that the basic reproduction number, which is denoted (R0) and corresponds to the average number of secondary infections caused by an infected individual (Anderson and May, 1991), is of the order of 3, which is consistent with estimates for the French epidemic (Salje et al., 2020; Sofonea et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Salje et al., 2020 and Sofonea et al., 2021.

claim: The uncontrolled epidemics in Epidemap simulations last 308 days with a 95% confidence interval of [286;345] days.
source: These uncontrolled epidemics last 308 days (95% confidence interval (CI): [286;345] days)
evidence: This is a result from the simulations.

claim: Geographical structure greatly impacts the unfolding of the epidemic.
source: This shows that geographical structure greatly impacts the unfolding of the epidemic.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the comparison between simulation results and mean-field predictions.

claim: The first peak in the national prevalence corresponds to the spread in the region where the outbreak emerges (Ile-de-France).
source: The first peak corresponds to the spread in the region where the outbreak emerges (here the Ile-de-France), whereas the second corresponds to the sum of the epidemic peaks in the other regions.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the simulation results shown in Figure 2.

claim: The second peak in the national prevalence corresponds to the sum of the epidemic peaks in regions other than the outbreak origin.
source: The first peak corresponds to the spread in the region where the outbreak emerges (here the Ile-de-France), whereas the second corresponds to the sum of the epidemic peaks in the other regions.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the simulation results shown in Figure 2.

claim: The bimodal structure of the epidemic is particularly pronounced because of the high population density in the region of origin of the outbreak (Ile-de-France).
source: This bimodal structure is particularly pronounced because of the high population density in the region of origin of the outbreak (Ile-de-France), but it is a direct consequence of the detailed geographical information in the simulation platform.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the simulation results.

claim: The bimodal structure of the epidemic is a direct consequence of the detailed geographical information in the simulation platform.
source: This bimodal structure is particularly pronounced because of the high population density in the region of origin of the outbreak (Ile-de-France), but it is a direct consequence of the detailed geographical information in the simulation platform.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the simulation results.

claim: In a well-mixed setting, the transmission model parameters yield a single epidemic peak.
source: As expected, in a well-mixed setting the parameters used for the transmission model yield a single peak (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The date of onset of the epidemic in an area strongly depends on its distance from the origin (Paris).
source: In Figure 3a, we show that the date of onset of the epidemic in an area strongly depends on its distance from the origin (here assumed to be Paris).
evidence: This is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 3a.

claim: There is an additional effect of density such that denser areas are infected first.
source: Furthermore, there is an additional effect of density such that denser areas are infected first.
evidence: This is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 3.

claim: At the departmental level, the trends of distance and density effects on epidemic onset are not significant.
source: Interestingly, at the departmental level, these trends are not significant, further showing the importance of a fine-grain simulation level.
evidence: This is a result from the simulations.

claim: The total proportion of inhabitants of a district who have been infected at the end of the epidemic strongly increases with density.
source: Furthermore, the total proportion of inhabitants of a district who have been infected at the end of the epidemic strongly increases with density.
evidence: This is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 3.

claim: The pandemic propagation velocity increases with time.
source: The pandemic propagation velocity also increases with time.
evidence: This is a result from the simulations.

claim: When incidence is high, long-distance dispersion events are not rare anymore, which biases the mean distance of contamination towards higher values.
source: This can be explained by the fact that, when incidence is high, long-distance dispersion events are not rare anymore, which biases the mean distance of contamination towards higher values.
evidence: This is an explanation for the observed increase in propagation velocity.

claim: For densely populated districts, the proportion of infected individuals converges towards the mean-field prediction from well-mixed models.
source: For densely populated districts (Figure 3b), this proportion converges towards the mean-field prediction from well-mixed models mentioned above (Kermack and McKendrick, 1927).
evidence: This is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 3b and a citation to Kermack and McKendrick, 1927.

claim: If the population density is low, the proportion of infected individuals is more variable, showing the limit of classical assumptions.
source: However, if the population density is low, this proportion is more variable showing the limit of classical assumptions.
evidence: This is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 3.

claim: Early in the epidemic, the distribution of individual reproduction numbers is tightly centred around the R0 value.
source: Early in the epidemic, the distribution is tightly centred around the R0 value (Figure 4a).
evidence: This is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 4a.

claim: As the epidemic unfolds, the distribution of individual reproduction numbers changes with a mode that decreases towards 0 and wider dispersal.
source: As the epidemic unfolds, the distribution changes with a mode that decreases towards 0, and a wider dispersal.
evidence: This is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 4.

claim: During the end of the epidemic, there is a general trend towards a decrease in super-spreading events.
source: During the end of the epidemic, stochasticity is strong but there is a general trend towards a decrease in super-spreading events.
evidence: This is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 4.

claim: Studies attempting to quantify the importance of superspreading events should account for the stage of the epidemic they analyse.
source: This is already sufficient to show that studies attempting to quantify the importance of superspreading events should account for the stage of the epidemic they analyse.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the simulation results.

claim: For SARS-CoV-2, clinical dynamics have little effect on transmission dynamics due to the life-history of the infection.
source: As expected in the case of SARS-CoV-2, where clinical dynamics have little effect on transmission dynamics due to the life-history of the infection (see the Materials and methods), these dynamics closely follow that of infection cases.
evidence: This is stated as an expectation based on the infection model described in Materials and methods.

claim: A two-waves epidemic pattern emerges at the French national level, which is largely driven by temporally shifted dynamics at the regional level.
source: First, a two-waves epidemic pattern emerges at the French national level, which is largely driven by temporally shifted dynamics at the regional level.
evidence: This is a summary of simulation results.

claim: Districts are affected by the epidemic depending on how far they are from the epicentre and their density.
source: Second, we find that districts are affected by the epidemic depending on how far they are from the epicentre, but also depending on their density.
evidence: This is a summary of simulation results.

claim: The density effect on epidemic timing is absent at the departmental level.
source: The latter effect is absent at the departmental level, which illustrates the added value of a detailed geographical structure.
evidence: This is a summary of simulation results.

claim: The simplistic estimate of the final epidemic size as a function of R0 does not apply at the national level.
source: Furthermore, as expected (Keeling, 1999), the simplistic estimate of the final epidemic size as a function of R0 does not apply at the national level.
evidence: This is supported by simulation results and a citation to Keeling, 1999.

claim: The simplistic estimate of the final epidemic size as a function of R0 does yield relevant results at the district level if the density is sufficiently high.
source: Conversely, this estimate does yield relevant results at the district level if the density is sufficiently high.
evidence: This is supported by simulation results.

claim: Super-spreading events become increasingly important as the epidemic unfolds.
source: Finally, being able to perform individual follow-ups allow us to see that super-spreading events become increasingly important as the epidemic unfolds, but that their role decreases as the importance of stochastic processes increase again at the end of the epidemic wave.
evidence: This is supported by simulation results.

claim: The role of super-spreading events decreases as the importance of stochastic processes increase again at the end of the epidemic wave.
source: Finally, being able to perform individual follow-ups allow us to see that super-spreading events become increasingly important as the epidemic unfolds, but that their role decreases as the importance of stochastic processes increase again at the end of the epidemic wave.
evidence: This is supported by simulation results.

claim: The link between the final size of the epidemic in a district and its population density appears strongly in SARS-CoV-2 data.
source: For instance, the link we identify between the final size of the epidemic in a district and its population density is not reported in the other ABS we discussed here, but appears quite strongly in SARS-CoV-2 data (Smith et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Smith et al., 2021.

claim: Superspreading events increase the risk of stochastic extinction but also fuel the speed of spread of epidemics that do emerge.
source: Similarly, superspreading events are known to be an important target for public policies because they increase the risk of stochastic extinction but also to fuel the speed of spread of epidemics that do emerge (Lloyd-Smith et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Lloyd-Smith et al., 2005.

claim: Field studies find that the importance of superspreading events may vary over the course of an epidemic.
source: However, although field studies find that their importance may vary over the course of an epidemic (Lau et al., 2017), we are not aware of an in-depth analysis of these emerging trends using ABS.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Lau et al., 2017.

claim: Individual movements based on a distance kernel centered in residency home is relevant for France.
source: As shown by earlier work on influenza dynamics, although this assumption is relevant for France, it might be too simplistic for countries like the United States, where air traffic represents a greater proportion of the travels (Crépey and Barthélemy, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Crépey and Barthélemy, 2007.

claim: The distance kernel assumption might be too simplistic for countries like the United States, where air traffic represents a greater proportion of travels.
source: As shown by earlier work on influenza dynamics, although this assumption is relevant for France, it might be too simplistic for countries like the United States, where air traffic represents a greater proportion of the travels (Crépey and Barthélemy, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Crépey and Barthélemy, 2007.

claim: Epidemap allows authorities to derive a risk factor per district to help control an epidemic and prevent outbreaks.
source: For instance, they allow authorities to derive a risk factor per district to help control an epidemic and prevent outbreaks.
evidence: This is a stated application of the simulation platform.

claim: Epidemap can simulate hospitalisations by sending an individual to the nearest hospital, allowing anticipation of ICU saturation at a detailed geographical level.
source: From an even more applied perspective, Epidemap can readily simulation hospitalisations by sending an individual to the nearest hospital, thereby allowing to anticipate the saturation of ICU at a detailed geographical level.
evidence: This is a stated capability of the simulation platform.

claim: Epidemap can be instrumental to optimise vaccine coverage in the context of the SARS-CoV-2 pandemic.
source: In the context of the SARS-CoV-2 pandemic, this simulation platform can also be instrumental to optimise vaccine coverage but also compare the effect of specific Non-Pharmaceutical Intervention (NPI) (e.g. mask-wearing vs. stay-at-home requirements).
evidence: This is a stated potential application of the simulation platform.

claim: Epidemap can compare the effect of specific Non-Pharmaceutical Interventions such as mask-wearing versus stay-at-home requirements.
source: In the context of the SARS-CoV-2 pandemic, this simulation platform can also be instrumental to optimise vaccine coverage but also compare the effect of specific Non-Pharmaceutical Intervention (NPI) (e.g. mask-wearing vs. stay-at-home requirements).
evidence: This is a stated potential application of the simulation platform.

claim: The OSM database has high accuracy in France because the official national land registry (Cadastre) database is merged into it.
source: The accuracy of this database is partially high in France because the official national land registry (the 'Cadastre') database is merged into the OSM database.
evidence: This is stated as a fact about the data source.

claim: The OSM database for France is approximately 80 GB in size.
source: These databases are formatted in ASCII XML, with a size of approximately 80 GB for France.
evidence: This is a description of the data used.

claim: The initial OSM database contains 4.1×10^8 nodes and 4.8×10^7 buildings.
source: In our current simulations, the initial database size contains 4.1 108 nodes and 4.8 107 buildings that need to be pre-processed to compute additional characteristics such as building surface, usage, or geographical location, which can be reused in different simulations.
evidence: This is a description of the data used.

claim: Each person is assumed to visit two distant buildings per day based on results from Schneider et al., 2013.
source: Following the results from the study on individual movement patterns by Schneider et al., 2013, we assume that each person can visit two distant buildings per day (where it can meet other agents).
evidence: This assumption is supported by a citation to Schneider et al., 2013.

claim: The log-normal parameterisation for distance yields results very consistent with INSEE data.
source: As shown in Table 1, this parameterisation yields results that are very consistent with the INSEE data (INSEE, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by comparison with INSEE data shown in Table 1.

claim: The maximum number of interactions is limited to 17 persons in a distant building and five in a residential building.
source: The maximum number of interactions is limited to 17 persons in a distant building and five in a residential building.
evidence: This is a description of the model parameters.

claim: For SARS-CoV-2, 95% of secondary infections occur within the first 11 days post-infection.
source: Indeed, data shows that patients are typically hospitalised 2 weeks after infection. Of the secondary infections, 95% occur within the first 11 days post-infection.
evidence: This is stated as a fact from data.

claim: Only a small fraction of hosts are hospitalised (less than 1% in France).
source: Furthermore, only a small fraction of the hosts are hospitalised (less than 1% in France O'Driscoll et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to O'Driscoll et al., 2021.

claim: Epidemap runs with less than 64 GB RAM for 6.6×10^7 agents.
source: A huge effort was made to reduce the memory print of the code, which runs with less than 64 GB Random Access Memory (RAM) for 6.6 107 agents.
evidence: This is a description of the computational performance.

claim: A full epidemic simulation of approximately 300 days is performed in 2 hours on a standard personal computer (12-cores AMD Ryzen 9).
source: A full epidemic simulation, which represents approximately 300 days, is performed in 2 hr on a standard personal computer (12-cores AMD Ryzen 9).
evidence: This is a description of the computational performance.

claim: OpenABM takes 1.5 seconds on a 2019 MacBookPro to simulate 1 day of epidemics for 1 million individuals.
source: The recent OpenABM platform (Hinch et al., 2021) is very transparent about its computation times: takes 1.5 s a 2019 MacBookPro (2.4 GHz Quad-Core Intel Core i5) to simulate 1 day of epidemics for 1 million individuals.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Hinch et al., 2021.

claim: To perform the study described (100 simulations of 66 million agents during a year), OpenABM would require approximately 40 days of computing time instead of approximately 8 days with Epidemap.
source: To perform our study (100 simulations of 66 million of agents during a year), the computing time would be ≈40 days instead of ≈8 days with Epidemap.
evidence: This is a comparison calculation based on the stated performance of OpenABM.

claim: The memory required to store transmission chain data for contact-tracing in OpenABM is approximately 3 kB per agent per epidemic week simulated.
source: For instance, the memory required to store the transmission chain data for the contact-tracing component of OpenABM is ≈3 kB per agent per epidemic week simulated.
evidence: This is stated as a fact about OpenABM's memory requirements.

claim: For one Epidemap run (66 million agents during one year), OpenABM would require more than 10 TB of RAM.
source: For one of our runs, that is the simulation of 66 million agents during one year, this would require more than 10 TB of RAM, which is clearly beyond the capabilities of a standard computer.
evidence: This is a calculation based on OpenABM's stated memory requirements.

claim: 66 million inhabitants of metropolitan France are explicitly mapped to housing buildings following cartographic and demographic data.
source: (A) The 66 millions inhabitants of metropolitan France are explicitly mapped to housing buildings following cartographic and demographic data.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1A.

claim: At each time point of the simulation, the number of infected individuals in each building of the country is recorded, as well as the time past since each got infected.
source: (B) At each time point of the simulation, the number of infected individuals in each building of the country is recorded, as well as the time past since each got infected (the panel shows the Paris area).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Every day, individuals can randomly move from their home to other buildings according to a mobility kernel and meet other people.
source: (C) Every day, individuals can randomly move from their home to other buildings according to a mobility kernel and meet other people.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1C.

claim: If an infected individual encounters a susceptible host, a transmission event can occur.
source: If an infected individual encounters a susceptible host, a transmission event can occur.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The contagiousness of an infected individual varies depending on the time since infection.
source: (D) The contagiousness of a infected individual varies depending on the time since infection.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1D.

claim: More than 95% of secondary transmission events occur before hospital admission.
source: Clinical dynamics can be assumed not to affect transmission dynamics because more than 95% of the secondary transmission events occur before hospital admission.
evidence: This is stated in Figure 1E caption.

claim: The daily estimates for the temporal reproduction number calculated at the individual level are very similar to those estimated using daily case incidence data and the method from Wallinga and Lipsitch, 2007.
source: Furthermore, the daily estimates for the temporal reproduction number calculated in the same manner are very similar to those estimated using the daily case incidence data (dashed blue curve) and the method from Wallinga and Lipsitch, 2007.
evidence: This comparison is supported by a citation to Wallinga and Lipsitch, 2007.

claim: Susceptible individuals are exposed to viral transmission from contagious individuals.
source: Susceptible individuals (yellow figurine), are exposed to viral transmission from contagious individuals (pink figurine).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5.
